tasks.label: Flip Box
tasks.description: Push the box toward a fixture and flip it upright.
tasks.insight: Maintaining contact matters as the contact point and force direction change.

tasks.label: Insert EV Charger
tasks.description: Align the EV charger with the socket and insert it.
tasks.insight: Insertion requires substantial force in the correct direction; misalignment can trigger overload errors.

tasks.label: Insert Peg
tasks.description: Grasp a peg, align it with the hole, and insert it.
tasks.insight: The 0.02 mm tolerance makes alignment and force direction critical.

tasks.label: Wipe Curve
tasks.description: Wipe along a curved surface to remove the marked regions.
tasks.insight: Sustained contact and appropriate force direction help remove marks along the curve.

backbones.adaptation: Task-adapted; adaptation type not specified in Table I

figures.alt: FP2 framework: a robotic foundation model generates actions, a compressor summarizes its context, and a force-control policy uses that context plus wrench and proprioceptive history to regulate execution. Below are the three training stages.
figures.caption: Figure 2. FP2 separates task-level action generation from force regulation. Training adapts the foundation model, learns contextual compression, then trains the force-control policy.

figures.alt: Four robot task sequences: flipping a box, inserting an EV charger, inserting a peg with 0.02 mm tolerance, and wiping a curved surface. Side panels illustrate contact and force-direction challenges.
figures.caption: Figure 3. Four contact-rich tasks test changing contact, directed insertion force, tight-tolerance alignment, and sustained surface contact.

figures.alt: Rollout images and measured force traces compare foundation policies with and without FP2 on all four tasks, illustrating contact loss or insufficient force versus regulated interaction.
figures.caption: Figure 4. Representative executions show how FP2 maintains contact and regulates insertion and wiping forces; these are qualitative examples, not aggregate success rates.

figures.alt: Stacked outcome bars for Flip Box and Insert EV Charger compare four backbones with and without FP2, separating success, position errors, and interaction-related failures across 25 trials each.
figures.caption: Figure 5. Failure breakdowns distinguish position errors from interaction-related causes on Flip Box and Insert EV Charger.

figures.alt: An orange training box and four novel objects varying in color, texture, stiffness, and geometry, including a purple box, a patterned blue box, a wooden box, and a yellow tapered container.
figures.caption: Table II, right panel. Training and novel objects for the Flip Box generalization evaluation.

SR.label: Success rate
SR.definition: Percentage of trials that successfully complete the task; used for Flip Box, Insert EV Charger, and Insert Peg.

CR.label: Completion rate
CR.definition: Fraction of marked regions successfully wiped clean, expressed as a percentage; a continuous completion metric, not binary task success.

NFE.label: Normalized Force Error
NFE.definition: Root mean square of 3D force deviations outside the demonstration mean ± one standard deviation, normalized by demonstrated variability after temporal normalization.
NFE.eligibility: Successful trials only; for Wipe Curve, successful continuous-wiping executions only. Null means no valid successful execution is available, not zero error.

average.label: Average score
average.definition: Arithmetic mean of the four task metrics (three SR values and one CR value), shown as the integer printed in Table I.

latency.label: Inference latency
latency.definition: Force-control policy latency per inference on an NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU.

caveats: RFM means robotic foundation model. FP2 regulates physical interaction; it does not replace task-level action generation or geometric reasoning.
Scores and averages reproduce the paper's rounded percentages; do not replace Table II's 88% novel-object score with 87.5%.
The initial comparison uses π0 with LoRA: average score 15% to 80%, a gain of 65 percentage points, not 65 percent relative improvement.
NFE compares successful execution subsets and must not be interpreted as an all-trial error or a success probability.
A nonzero Wipe Curve completion rate can coexist with unavailable NFE, because partial completion does not imply a successful continuous-wiping execution.
TA-VLA and ForceVLA use the matched π0 LoRA comparison from Table I; separate full-fine-tuning experiments in the prose are not mixed into these values.
Table I is on physical PDF page 7. Figures 4 and 5 and Table II are on physical PDF page 6 in the supplied file.
